source.title: Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders
source.authors: Leo Gao; Tom Dupré la Tour; Henk Tillman; Gabriel Goh; Rajan Troll; A. Radford; I. Sutskever; Jan Leike; Jeffrey Wu

record.tranche_reason: Applies sparse autoencoders to GPT-2 small and GPT-4 activations and reports feature-recovery and feature-quality results relevant to indirect evidence for sparse features in language models. It does not reproduce or directly test the toy-model superposition result.
record.gate_note: The paper reports probe, explanation, and ablation-effect measurements on SAE latents. General SAE reconstruction/scaling results and cited results from other work are not included unless they bear on a listed claim version.
record.test_reason: An SAE scaling and methods paper on GPT-2 small and GPT-4. Most of its results are about its own method's performance (TopK vs ReLU, MSE scaling), which is T4-like. Some results do bear on V4 and V5. Single SAE latents recover task labels better than residual-stream channels (0.600 baseline on GPT-4). Latent ablation effects are much sparser than channel ablations (10-14% vs 60%). The authors also give stated limits on monosemanticity and completeness.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors' central conclusion is that TopK SAEs give clean scaling laws and few dead latents. Their feature-quality metrics (probe recovery, explainability, ablation sparsity) generally improve with SAE size. Increasing L0 helps probe loss and ablation sparsity but hurts token-pattern explanations, and all trends break as L0 nears d_model. They acknowledge many GPT-4 latents are not yet adequately monosemantic.
record.recipe_differences: Trains and evaluates sparse autoencoders on language-model activations; does not implement the toy-model feature-superposition method or directly measure toy-network feature geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature-quality results depend on SAE size and active-latent count k; the paper reports worse interpretability and less sparse ablation effects as k approaches dmodel.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE encoder directions split into two fuzzy subspaces of about 25% and 75% of dimensions. The smaller cluster has latents active on fewer than 100 vocabulary tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: GPT-2 small residual stream decomposes into distinct subspaces with different feature types.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger GPT-4-family subject models need more latents for the same MSE, with a worse exponent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The number of sparse features needed scales with subject model size.

record.problems: Several relevant results are reported only as plots without numeric values. Probe evaluation relies on the authors' curated task set and is described as noisy; N2G explanations capture only simple patterns. The authors also note that many GPT-4 random activations are not adequately monosemantic.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded general SAE MSE and compute-scaling results, training-method comparisons not directly measuring feature recovery or geometry, and cited findings from prior studies. No relevant results were omitted for the 12-row cap.

untested.parts: No toy models; geometry and the sparsity phase transition are not tested.
No test of capacity competition as the cause of polysemanticity.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
Does not measure whether features are distributed across many neurons, beyond the channel baselines.
No seed-to-seed stability test, and no test of whether SAE features are canonical across dictionary sizes.
No test of 1-D vs multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: With the 16M SAE substituted into GPT-4, LM loss matches a model trained with 10% of GPT-4 pretraining compute; zero-ablation fidelity is 98.2%.
An irreducible loss term is needed in the scaling fits. Random Gaussian data gives an L(N) exponent of -0.04 vs about -0.26 for GPT-2 activations.
Metrics vary by layer: earlier layers give better N2G explanations, later layers better probe loss and logit sparsity (k=32, n=32768).
The same dense latents (position, first-token, repetition) recur across GPT-2 SAEs trained differently. Opposing near-antipodal latents are conjectured to be optimization failures.
A qualitative report that most GPT-2 small latents seemed interpretable on random activations.
7% of latents are dead in the 16M SAE.

record.verdict_notes: Borderline T4: most of the paper evaluates the authors' own SAE method. The bearing on V4 rests mainly on the residual-channel baselines. The original source (Toy Models, arXiv:2209.10652) is cited only for the subspace idea.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network experiment tests superposition, feature overlap, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry.
Does not test whether polysemanticity results from capacity competition, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
Does not test whether polysemanticity arises for reasons other than capacity pressure or whether it is evidence of superposition.
Tests whether SAE latents recover selected features or yield interpretable explanations in GPT-2 small and GPT-4. Does not test the claim that features are spread across many neurons.
Evaluates feature recovery and interpretability, but does not test feature stability across training runs or whether SAE features are canonical units.
Does not compare one-dimensional and multidimensional feature representations or test the dimensionality of underlying model features.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Trained a one-dimensional logistic probe on each SAE latent for each task and recorded the best cross-entropy loss across latents.

conditions.value: number of latents n and active latents k varied

rows.measure: Best one-dimensional probe cross-entropy loss for recovering task labels
rows.baseline: Direct residual-stream channels are stated to perform substantially worse; numeric value not stated here
rows.value: Probe score increases and then decreases as k increases; figure-only values
rows.note: The authors state that TopK generally achieves better probe scores than ReLU and that both are substantially better than using residual-stream channels directly. The result varies with k.
rows.check: Authors say SAE latents are substantially better than residual-stream channels. The non-monotonic k dependence is a scope condition, not a weaker effect. No numeric values are given (figure only).

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Measured how well Neuron to Graph explanations capture SAE latent activations.

conditions.value: number of latents n and active latents k varied

rows.measure: N2G explanation quality, including precision and recall
rows.value: Authors state that more total latents and fewer active latents generally make latents easiest to model with N2G; figure-only values
rows.note: The paper also notes that n=2048, k=512 latents are easy to explain because many activate densely.
rows.check: There is no baseline, so it cannot show V4's effect. It bears on V5 only: explainability depends on n and k, and is inflated by dense latents at k=512.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.3; Section E.5, Figure 21 caption; Figure 25 caption.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Compared N2G explanations for TopK and ReLU autoencoders.

conditions.value: TopK versus ReLU, with the same n and similar L0

rows.value: TopK has recall greater than 1.5x and precision greater than 0.9x relative to ReLU; the paper states F1 is better
rows.note: Recall improves substantially while precision is slightly worse.
rows.check: This compares the study's own method against ReLU SAEs. It is a method comparison, not a measure of whether sparse features exist or are canonical.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Simulated SAE latents from N2G explanations, decoded them, and measured downstream language-model loss.

conditions.value: number of latents n and active latents k varied

rows.measure: Downstream loss after decoding N2G-simulated latent values
rows.baseline: Bigrams and residual-stream ablations are shown as comparisons; numeric values not stated
rows.value: Authors state larger and sparser autoencoders give better downstream loss, and that they explain more of GPT-2 small than just explaining bigrams; figure-only values
rows.note: This metric combines explanation quality with downstream performance, but the text does not report that the explanations fully account for the model.
rows.check: Explanations do better than bigrams but do not fully recover the model's loss. Figure only.

source_check.correct: Split the state by version: observed for V4's recoverable-feature evidence; partial for V5's completeness. N2G explanations capture more GPT-2-small performance than bigrams, with better downstream loss for larger, sparser SAEs; complete recovery is not reported.
source_check.problem: A shared partial state conflates incomplete model explanation under V5 with V4, which does not require complete recovery.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Ablated individual SAE latents and measured the sparsity of their effects on output logits.
rows.measure: Normalized effective number of vocabulary tokens affected by a latent ablation
rows.value: SAE latent effects are 10-14%; larger k generally gives sparser effects, but the trend reverses at k=512
rows.note: The paper says latents have sparse effects in an absolute sense, while the result worsens as k approaches dmodel=768.
rows.check: 10-14% vs 60% for channel ablations is a clear effect. The reversal at k=512 is a scope condition.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Measured the average density of the dmodel densest SAE latents.
rows.measure: Average density of the dmodel densest features, divided by L0
rows.value: Dense-latent solutions begin around k=256; figure-only density value
rows.note: The authors describe k=256, n=2048 as a possible intermediate regime.
rows.check: This is a hyperparameter-dependent dense regime, an SAE solution property. It is not evidence about sparse features in the LM itself, so V4 is removed.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Measured the average density of the dmodel densest SAE latents.
rows.measure: Average density of the dmodel densest features, divided by L0
rows.value: Many learned latents are dense; figure-only density value
rows.note: The paper associates this regime with less interpretable features, scaling-law breaks, and ablations no longer having sparse effects.
rows.check: Same as R9: the dense solutions at k=512 show that the SAE's learned units depend on k. V4 is removed.

rows.subject: GPT-4
rows.operation_detail: Authors assessed random positive SAE-latent activations for monosemanticity.
rows.value: The authors state that a large fraction of random activations, especially in GPT-4, are not yet adequately monosemantic
rows.note: This is a stated qualitative limitation; no fraction or quantitative evaluation is given.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Clustered SAE encoder directions by their projections on singular-vector bases.

conditions.value: SVD-based ordering and one-dimensional UMAP embedding

rows.measure: Distribution of SAE latents and dimensions across inferred subspaces
rows.value: Two fuzzily separated subspaces: about 25% of latents mostly project on about 25% of dimensions; the remaining 75% mostly project on the remaining 75%
rows.note: This describes SAE encoder-direction clustering, not a test of whether underlying superposed features are one- or multidimensional.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked. This is SAE encoder subspace structure, not a test of V6.

relationships.condition: GPT-4 (128k/1M/16M SAEs) and GPT-2 small layer 8, single-latent probes and ablation sparsity
relationships.reason: Single SAE latents recover curated task labels better than residual channels (baseline 0.600), with scores improving through unsupervised training. Latent ablations affect 10-14% of effective tokens vs 60% for channels (R1-R4, R8).
relationships.display_finding: Single SAE latents recovered curated task labels better than residual channels (baseline 0.600), and scores improved over unsupervised training. Latent ablations affected 10–14% of effective tokens versus 60% for channels.

relationships.condition: GPT-2 small SAEs with k approaching d_model (k=512), and choice of layer
relationships.reason: Probe score rises then falls with k, and ablation sparsity reverses at k=512 (R1, R8). Per the text, later layers recover features better while earlier layers explain better (Fig. 28).
relationships.display_finding: Probe score rose and then fell as k increased, and ablation sparsity reversed at k=512. Later layers recovered features better, while earlier layers explained better.

source_check.reason: Probe quality depends nonmonotonically on k, and the ablation-sparsity trend reverses at k=512 (R1, R8). Section F.1 and Figure 28 show different layer dependencies for explanation, recovery, and ablation metrics.

relationships.condition: GPT-4 random activations; GPT-2 small dense regimes (k=256-512); N2G explanations
relationships.reason: Authors state a large fraction of GPT-4 random activations are not adequately monosemantic (R11). At high k the SAE learns dense, less interpretable latents (R9, R10). Explanation quality depends on n and k (R5, R7).
relationships.display_finding: The authors state a large fraction of GPT-4 random activations are not adequately monosemantic; at high k, GPT-2 small SAEs learned dense, less interpretable latents, and explanation quality varied with n and k.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: GPT-4 random activations; GPT-2 small dense regimes (k=256-512); N2G explanations
source_check.reason: The authors explicitly report inadequate monosemanticity for many random GPT-4 activations (R11). Dense, less interpretable SAE solutions emerge with large k, and explanation quality depends on dictionary size and sparsity (R5, R7, R9, R10). These qualify the learned dictionaries without establishing universal failure.

relationships.reason: From the text, not rows. Substituting the 16M SAE gives loss equal to a model trained with 10% of GPT-4's compute, and the scaling fits need an irreducible loss term. The dictionary is therefore incomplete.
relationships.display_finding: Substituting the 16M-latent SAE gave loss equal to a model trained with 10% of GPT-4's compute, and the scaling fits required an irreducible loss term.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Section 4.1 reports substituted-model loss equivalent to a model trained with 10% of GPT-4's compute, supporting incompleteness of this trained dictionary. The irreducible term improves empirical fits; it does not prove an unavoidable reconstruction floor.
